The closure rule and trap principleThe proof uses the following precise rule. Write  $\mu_M$  for the actual-mate involution, let  $I\subseteq\{p,q\}$  be the granted sites, and let  $F_t\subseteq P^*$  be the endpoints frozen by time  $t$ . Then
$$F_0=\varnothing,\qquad
F_{t+1}
=
F_t\cup
\left\{
v\in P^*:
\left|N(v)\cap\bigl(T^*\cup I\cup\mu_M(F_t)\bigr)\right|\ge2
\right\},$$
where  $N(v)$  denotes the nearest-neighbour sites.Under this rule, the first-member trap principle is valid: if a nonempty  $S\subseteq P^*$  satisfies
$$\left|N(v)\cap
\bigl(T^*\cup I\cup\mu_M(P^*\setminus S)\bigr)\right|
\le1
\qquad(v\in S),$$
then no member of  $S$  belongs to the least freezing closure. At the hypothetical first freezing event in  $S$ , every previously frozen endpoint lies outside  $S$ , so the displayed bound prevents that event.This formulation confirms that the argument properly accounts for actual mates. It grants the strongest possible assistance from endpoints outside the trap, so circular dependencies outside or across the proposed trap cannot invalidate the obstruction.Colour separation also holds exactly. An endpoint’s neighbours have the opposite colour, and their actual mates have the endpoint’s own colour. Thus the white and black closure problems can be processed independently. The grant  $p$  affects black endpoints only, and  $q$  affects white endpoints only.2. Forced cores, interval traps, and tail trapsThe  $EF$  obstruction is valid for arbitrary matchingsIf  $EF$  is absent, the available endpoint mates of  $A,C,E$  all lie in
$$S=\{B,U,D\}.$$
Because the matching is perfect, these three black vertices exhaust the three white vertices of  $S$ .At  $B$ , every endpoint-neighbour’s mate remains in  $S$ . At  $U$ , only  $V$  can have a mate outside  $S$ ; at  $D$ , only  $G$  can. None of  $B,U,D$  has a selected or granted neighbour. Hence  $S$  is a first-member trap.This establishes the forced- $EF$  reduction independently of the later template classification.With  $EF$  fixed, the five internal vertices of
$$V-U-A-B-C-D-G$$
have no remaining endpoint neighbours outside this path. Exactly one of its two ends must be matched into the path. The resulting possibilities are precisely
$$L:\ UV,AB,CD,
\qquad
R:\ AU,BC,DG.$$
